# Introduction

It is important to this project to engage with our communities to share what we are learning and also learn from each of you. If you are receiving this Informational Sheet, it means you have expressed interest in conducting a home baking evaluation using a new perennial variety of rye. Thank you! This sheet is meant to give you more in-depth information about this new variety, so you can decide if you would like to participate.

# An overview of the project

As a citizen scientist, you will be given approximately 1 kg of rye flour from a new perennial variety. You will need to purchase any additional ingredients you need to do your baking. You will be asked to take notes during your baking and use them to fill out a follow-up survey. Upon completion of the follow-up survey, you will be sent a small thank you gift (see Figure 1).

In 2027, during the summer the project will also host an event where you can see the perennial rye variety growing in the field in a test plot in Jutland, and in the fall there will be a public symposium in Copenhagen to share current knowledge about perennial rye with everyone across the value chain (researchers, breeders, farmers, millers, bakers, and bread eaters). The events are freely open to the public - your attendance is welcome but optional.

# Funding and project partners

This citizen science project is part of a NNF Plant2Food research project (Grant #NNF22SA0081019) being conducted at the [Department of Agroecology](https://agro.au.dk/en/) and [Department of Food Science](https://food.au.dk/) at Aarhus University in Denmark in collaboration [Wageningen University and Research](https://www.wur.nl/en/persons/lr-laura-righetti) in the Netherlands, and with [Meyers](https://meyers.dk/), a prominent Danish food enterprise.

# Answers to some common questions

### Is it safe to eat?

Yes. The grain used to make the flour you are receiving was tested at an independent laboratory to ensure it is safe for human consumption. You can access the lab results \[here — link to be added\] and they will be sent to you along with the flour.

### Is this perennial rye variety genetically modified using new breeding technologies?

No, this variety was developed using traditional breeding methods, involving crossing plants by hand, and making selections based on their physical characteristics. You can read more about it in [this scientific publication from 1986](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1439-037X.1986.tb00077.x).

### Is this grain organic?

No, Aarhus University does not have any organically certified land due to the costs and additional administrative complexity that would entail. However, this grain was grown without the use of pesticides.

### Can I buy this flour somewhere?

Flour from this perennial rye variety is not currently available commercially. This project is laying the groundwork for a potential commercial release, and your help is appreciated!

# For the curious

This part was confusing to Matt - the kitchen garden and connection to the image weren\\t clear, and I think I should highlight the ANNUAL area, with better labels.

Broadly speaking, all plants fall roughly into two categories: perennial and annual. Perennial plants live for more than one year, while annual plants do not. In nature, perennial plants are very common. Think of a neighborhood park: there will be trees, grass, maybe some roses. These are all perennial plants. In contrast, many of the plants in your kitchen garden are annuals, meaning you have to re-plant them every year (for example radishes, lettuce, or cucumbers). This general pattern of ‘perennials in nature, annuals in agriculture’ is actually seen at a global scale. And while we do have a lot of wonderful perennial crops, the crops we use the most (and the ones we plant on the most land) are annuals.

![Globally, perennial plants are much more common compared to annuals. There is an over-representation of annuals in our agricultural crops, which is even more pronounced when you look at the area planted to annual versus perennial crops. Crops we use to make breads (wheat, barley, rye, maize, oats, sorghum, teff, millet, rice) are all annual crops. Figure created by Virginia Nichols.](images/figure-2.png){fig-cap="Figure 2." width="85%"}

Are annual plants just superior to perennials for food production? Did humans deliberately *choose* to domesticate annual crops? Or was it just coincidence? These questions are currently being debated. However, regardless of how we got here, it is clear that having more perennials integrated into our agricultural land would be good for the environment. This is because perennials tend to offer benefits to the overall environment; they help put carbon into the soil, they provide soil cover year-round, and they use resources like water and nitrogen more efficiently. Development of new perennial crops is one option, including perennial grains like the perennial rye used in this project.

STOPPED WITH MATT

Society has long recognized the potential benefits of a perennial grain. There have been efforts to breed perennial wheat in the Soviet Union since the 1930s! In the past, it has been a very difficult task, mainly because scientists had few tools to see what was going on inside the plant’s genetics. Despite these challenges, a few laboratories got lucky and had some successes, including one in Germany at the University of Hohenheim. There, Dr. Reimann-Philips and his team successfully crossed an annual rye with a perennial ancestor in the 1960s. The team tested the results, and made more selections. The resulting crop was perennial (Figure 3), and in 199X it was submitted to be considered as a variety in Germany.

![Annual bread rye is sown in the fall, and the crop dies in late summer before the grain is harvested. Perennial bread rye is also sown in the fall, and while the growth from that year dies and grain is harvested just like in the annual crop, the roots stay alive and the crop regrows once light can hit the base of the plant. This new growth acts just like a crop that is sown in the fall…except you didn’t have to sow it.](images/figure-3.png){fig-cap="Figure 3." width="85%"}

But…the government didn’t think anyone would want to grow such a crop, so it was pushed aside and became a side project. The breeders maintained some plots as their passion project, and while some of the material was later released as a wildlife forage crop, the perennial grain hasn’t gotten anyone’s full attention for the past thirty years. In 2023, Dr. Thomas Miedaner, who took over the University of Hohenheim’s rye breeding program after Dr. Reimann-Philips’ passing, shared some seeds of this neglected and forgotten crop with researchers at Aarhus University.

In 2025 we tested it side-by-side against a high-yielding annual rye. We were very impressed when it produced half of the grain yield of the modern annual, given that it was crossed with varieties from the 1960s! We think this variety deserves more development, and this grant is part of that effort. One of the goals of the grant is to understand how this new perennial bread rye performs in home kitchens, and to hear how people feel about this new perennial grain.

### How long would this crop continue to produce grain?

It has not been tested extensively at this point, but it seems the perennial cereal rye reliably produces grain for at least two years. After this time weeds and diseases may become problems, but we need more research to determine the optimal way to manage the crop.
